opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they're really at the heart of what we mean by intelligence. When we say a person understands something, part of what we mean is that they can take what they've learned in one situation and apply it flexibly in a new one that looks quite different on the surface. That requires forming abstractions: concepts that capture the essence of a situation and aren't tied to its particular details.

Humans do this all the time, often without noticing. A child who learns what "sameness" means with blocks can recognize it in sounds or in patterns of behavior. We understand a phrase like "she's the backbone of the team" without anyone teaching us that specific mapping. My own work going back to grad school, on the Copycat project with Douglas Hofstadter, was really about this: how do you perceive the deep structure of a situation so you can make an analogy to another one? I've come to believe that analogy-making and abstraction aren't side issues in cognition. They're fundamental to it.

Current AI systems, including the very impressive large models, are extraordinarily good at learning statistical patterns from enormous amounts of data. But we keep seeing that they can be brittle. They learn shortcuts, correlations in the training data that work on benchmarks but don't reflect the concept we actually wanted them to learn. Change the problem in a way that wouldn't bother a person at all, and performance can fall apart. That tells me they haven't formed the kind of abstractions we have. They've learned something, but it's not quite "the concept."

That matters practically too. If we want systems we can trust in the real world, which is messy, open-ended, and full of situations nobody anticipated in the training data, they have to be able to transfer what they know robustly. You can't enumerate every case. So for me, abstraction and transfer aren't just interesting research puzzles. They're where the gap between today's AI and genuine understanding really shows up. Things like Chollet's ARC challenge, and the work my group has done with variations on it, try to probe exactly that: can a system grasp a new concept from just a few examples, the way people can? So far that remains very hard for machines.

r001.rationale: It describes applying what was learned in one situation to a different one and explicitly connects this ability to analogy-making.

r002.rationale: It says systems must transfer what they know to handle messy, unanticipated real-world situations, linking this robust transfer to addressing brittleness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think abstraction is really at the heart of what we mean by intelligence. When I say abstraction, I mean the ability to take what you've learned in one situation and recognize that its essence applies to a new situation that might look quite different on the surface. Humans do this effortlessly, and even very young children do it. A child who learns what a dog is from a few examples can recognize a dog in a cartoon, a dog made of clay, a dog seen from a strange angle. They've captured something essential about "dogness" rather than memorizing surface features.

What we've seen with current AI systems, even the very impressive ones, is that they often learn in a way that's much more tied to the specific statistics of their training data. They can perform brilliantly within the distribution they were trained on, and then fail in surprising ways when something shifts a little. That's really a failure of abstraction. The system hasn't formed the kind of concept that would let it transfer.

And this matters enormously for robustness and trust. If I'm going to rely on a system in the real world, the real world is never going to look exactly like the training data. So transfer isn't a nice-to-have, it's the whole game. That's partly why I've been so interested in Francois Chollet's Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, because it tries to test exactly this: can you grasp a rule from a few examples and apply it to something new? And it's striking how hard that still is for machines, while being fairly natural for people.

I'd also say there's a deeper scientific question here. We don't really understand how humans form abstractions, how we build concepts that are flexible and compositional and grounded in analogy. My own earlier work with Douglas Hofstadter on Copycat was an attempt to model that kind of analogy-making. So for me, studying abstraction in AI is also a way of studying what concepts actually are, and I think until we make progress on that, we're going to keep being surprised by the brittleness of our systems.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying what was learned in one situation to a different one and separately mentions analogy-making, but it does not clearly characterize that transfer itself as a form of analogy.

r002.rationale: It calls transfer essential for real-world reliability and explains that applying learning to situations unlike the training data addresses AI systems’ brittleness.

astra-6.text:
Well, one of the most striking things about human intelligence is that we can take something we’ve learned in one situation and apply it in a situation that looks quite different. We don’t have to learn everything from scratch. And I think abstraction is a big part of what makes that possible: we can recognize that two situations share an underlying structure, even when their details are different.

For example, you can understand the idea of a bottleneck in traffic, and then recognize a bottleneck in an organization or in a computer program. Those are very different domains, but there’s a common pattern: something is restricting the flow. Recognizing that pattern lets you bring some of your previous understanding to the new situation.

AI systems can be very successful within the conditions they were trained on, yet fail when those conditions change in ways that seem insignificant to us. That raises the question: what did the system actually learn? Did it capture something general, or did it learn particular cues that happened to work during training?

So abstraction and transfer are closely connected. Abstraction is about capturing what matters beyond a particular example, and transfer is about being able to use that understanding somewhere else. If we want AI that can deal with genuinely new situations, those abilities have to be central.

r001.rationale: It describes recognizing a shared structure across different domains and applying prior understanding, illustrated by carrying the bottleneck idea from traffic to organizations or programs. This communicates analogy in substance.

r002.rationale: It says AI can fail when conditions change and identifies transfer as central to handling genuinely new situations, communicating how transfer can make systems less brittle.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one of the most striking things about human intelligence is that we can take something we’ve learned in one situation and apply it to a new situation that looks quite different on the surface. We’re able to recognize that there’s some underlying structure in common. And abstraction is really about capturing that structure—figuring out what matters and what details you can ignore.

For example, you can learn what it means to help someone, and recognize helping in all kinds of situations involving different people, different actions, even different goals. It’s not just a particular visual pattern. It’s a relationship between things.

AI systems can be extremely successful within the settings they’re trained on, but often struggle when the setting changes. That raises the question: What have they actually learned? Have they learned a general concept, or some features that happen to predict the right answer in their training data?

So I see abstraction and transfer as very closely connected. The ability to transfer gives us a way to probe whether a system has captured something more general. And if we want AI that can deal with new situations without having to be trained on every possible variation, then understanding how to form and use those abstractions is central.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying learning to a different situation and recognizing shared structure, but does not characterize that process as analogy or an equivalent relational mapping.

r002.rationale: It identifies transfer to new situations as central to AI that can handle changes without training on every variation, communicating how transfer can make systems less brittle.
